key_insight: A single deep-learning model jointly predicts bioactivity and reconstructs molecules to quantify when candidates lie outside the training distribution, enabling discovery of active kinase inhibitors at the 'edge' of chemical space.
problem_solved: Chemical ML models often fail when proposed molecules are far from the training set and lack principled ways to detect distribution shift; this work provides a method to identify out-of-distribution compounds and validate predictions experimentally.
method: Joint objective learning: shared molecular representation trained simultaneously for bioactivity prediction and molecular reconstruction to produce robust embeddings.

Principled distribution-shift scoring: use reconstruction / representation-based signals (and associated uncertainties) to quantify when a candidate is out-of-distribution (on the edge of chemical space).
Experimental validation loop: model-guided selection of compounds followed by biochemical assays that discovered active inhibitors for two clinically relevant kinase targets.
impact: Gives ML practitioners a practical framework to detect unreliable predictions and safely explore novel chemical regions, improving hit discovery efficiency and reducing wasted experiments when venturing beyond training data.
visual_elements: Schematic of the model: shared encoder with two heads (bioactivity predictor + molecule reconstructor).
Chemical-space map (e.g., UMAP) showing training distribution, edge compounds, and overlayed distribution-shift scores.
Performance vs. reliability plot: predictive accuracy + calibration/uncertainty metrics and experimental hit rates for in-distribution vs edge compounds.
Example molecular structures of discovered kinase inhibitors annotated with assay outcomes (to show real experimental validation).
paper_title: Molecular deep learning at the edge of chemical space
paper_authors: Derek van Tilborg, Luke Rossen, Francesca Grisoni
